title: Schools, census and marriages
text:
Keeping track of statistics and trends related to religion in Ireland, with data sourced mainly from the Central Statistics Office and the Department of Education. The code that reproduces every figure is on GitHub. The figures are interactive.
Part of Religion in Ireland. See also the Primary School Survey 2026 and the charities landscape.

title: Schools, census and marriages
section: The Catholic ethos enjoys a pronounced hegemony among primary schools in Ireland
text:
The Catholic ethos enjoys a pronounced hegemony among primary schools in Ireland


Figure 1. The vast majority of Irish mainstream primary schools have a Catholic ethos, followed by Church of Ireland. A far smaller minority follow an inter- or multi-denominational ethos. Hover over or tap a school for its name and county. Data: Department of Education, data on individual schools, using the latest list published; the map is checked for a new list every month. Code: make_maps.py. Open full screen.

title: Schools, census and marriages
section: Secular shift: Catholic marriages plummet as civil ceremonies surge
text:
Secular shift: Catholic marriages plummet as civil ceremonies surge


Figure 2. Opposite-sex marriages registered in Ireland by form of ceremony, 2000 to 2024. In 2000, 80% of marriages were Roman Catholic ceremonies and 16% were civil. By 2024 the two were level, at about 33% each, and Humanist ceremonies made up a further 7%. Data: CSO PxStat table VSA44. Code: fetch_marriage_cso.py, make_charts.py.

title: Schools, census and marriages
section: Age is no barrier: Catholicism declines as religious non-affiliation increases
text:
Age is no barrier: Catholicism declines as religious non-affiliation increases


Figure 3. Roman Catholic affiliation in Ireland by age group, census years 2011, 2016 and 2022. Affiliation declined in every age group. The steepest decline was among 25- to 34-year-olds (down 25 points), and the smallest among people aged 85 and over (down 4 points). Data: CSO PxStat table F5071.


Figure 4. The share of people stating no religion, by age group, census years 2011, 2016 and 2022. Data: CSO PxStat table F5071. Code for Figures 3 and 4: fetch_religion_cso.py, make_charts.py.

title: Religion in Ireland
text:
Over 90% of Irish primary schools are run by a religious patron, most of them Catholic, and the State’s auditor has found that 85% of schools are built on land owned by patrons or trustees. At the same time, fewer people say they’re Catholic at every census, and civil ceremonies are now as common as Catholic weddings.
This project tracks the place of religion in Irish public life using open data, mainly from the Central Statistics Office, the Department of Education and the Charities Regulator. The code behind every figure is on GitHub.

title: Fianaise
text:
Ireland publishes a great deal of open data, from the Central Statistics Office, government departments and public registers. Most of it sits in spreadsheets that journalists, policymakers and the public rarely have the time to dig through. Fianaise turns that data into charts, maps and short analysis, with the data and code behind every figure, so anyone can check it, cite it and reuse it.
Fianaise is Irish for evidence. The site is independent and unfunded, and everything on it is free to reuse.

title: About
text:
Fianaise takes open data about Irish public life and makes it readable: charts and maps, a few sentences on what they show, and the data and code behind each one. The aim is to keep the public informed and to help hold institutions to account, by doing the analysis that journalists and policymakers often don’t have the time to do.
Fianaise is Irish for evidence.

title: About
text:
Who I am
My name is Maedbh King. I’m a trained researcher, with a PhD from the University of California, Berkeley and a postdoctoral fellowship at MIT, and I work in strategy and policy at Trinity College Dublin. Fianaise is independent of my employer and is done in my own time.

title: About
text:
Corrections
If you spot a mistake, please open an issue on GitHub (there is a form for corrections). Corrections are made in the open, and the change history of every page is public on GitHub.

title: About
text:
Reuse
Text and figures are licensed CC BY 4.0: reuse them freely, with credit to Fianaise. Code is MIT licensed. The underlying data belongs to its publishers and keeps their licences (see Data & code).

title: Data & code
text: Every figure on Fianaise is built from public data by code in the fianaise.ie repository. The data belongs to its publishers and keeps their licences.

title: Data & code
text:
Code

analysis/education_equality: fetches the CSO and Department of Education data and draws the religion and survey figures.
analysis/charts: draws the census, marriage and survey charts and maps in the site’s style. tools/fetch_school_lists.py downloads new school lists from gov.ie, and a monthly GitHub Action uses it to redraw the maps and propose the update.
analysis/charities: builds the charities landscape from the Charities Regulator’s register.

title: The charities landscape
text:
Part of Religion in Ireland.
Every registered charity in Ireland, grouped by the charitable purposes it registered under, from the Charities Regulator’s register (26 October 2026). Charities for the advancement of religion are in orange. Schools with a Catholic ethos in the Department of Education lists are in blue, and community schools with a Catholic bishop or order as joint patron are in light blue. Schools register for education, not religion, so they sit inside the Education cluster. Hover over or tap a dot to read the charity’s objects.



Open the graphic full screen. How it was built, and the school matches to check before quoting a single school: analysis/charities.

title: Primary School Survey 2026
text:
Part of Religion in Ireland.
Over 90% of Irish primary schools are denominational, yet recent survey data (June 2026) shows substantial and widespread parental demand for multi-denominational education. The maps and graphs below explore that gap, school by school and county by county, with a particular focus on how the preferences of parents differ from those of school staff and boards of management.
The data comes from the Department of Education and Youth’s 2025–2026 Primary School Survey and its results summary report. The results for staff and boards of management are not in the spreadsheet the Department publishes, only in the summary report. The code is on GitHub. The figures are interactive.

title: Primary School Survey 2026
section: There is an unmet demand for multi-denominational primary schools in Ireland
text:
There is an unmet demand for multi-denominational primary schools in Ireland


Figure 1. Each primary school’s current ethos compared with the ethos its parents said they prefer. Hover over or tap a school for its survey results. Code: make_maps.py. Open full screen.

title: Primary School Survey 2026
section: Parents want multi-denominational education more than staff and boards of management
text:
Parents want multi-denominational education more than staff and boards of management


Figure 2. Percentage of households (with children in school, and with children not yet in school), and of staff and boards of management, who prefer multi-denominational education, in each county. Use the buttons to switch between household groups. Code: make_maps.py. Open full screen.






NoteHow the staff and board of management survey was run





The school staff and board of management survey was open to primary school staff and members of boards of management nationally. The target population was 84,285 staff and board members. A total of 32,999 responses were submitted, and 32,901 valid responses were kept after validation. That is a validated response rate of 39.0% of the eligible population. (Source: results summary report, section 4.1, p. 25.)

title: Primary School Survey 2026
section: There is a mismatch between the schools parents want for their children and the schools available to them
text:
There is a mismatch between the schools parents want for their children and the schools available to them


Figure 3. Stated ethos preference among households with a child not yet in school (n = 56,227), grouped by the type of school they intend to use. Each bar is 100% of the households intending that school type, split by whether they prefer a multi-denominational (green) or denominational (grey) ethos. This isolates demand for change: households intending a denominational school but preferring a multi-denominational one represent unmet demand, while households intending and preferring the same type represent confirmed preference. Percentages are recomputed from raw counts reported in the source, and the base (56,227) can’t be independently checked against the published survey spreadsheet. Source: Department of Education and Youth, Primary School Survey results summary report (June 2026), section 3.1.2, p. 14. Code: make_charts.py.
